title: What If the Moon Moved Twice as Close? The 8× Tide Surprise #shorts
description:
An evidence-based, idealized what-if: move the Moon to half its current average orbital distance while keeping its mass constant. Lunar tide-generating force scales with distance to the inverse third power, so the forcing rises eightfold. Actual local water heights do NOT become eight times larger by a simple rule; ocean geometry and resonance matter. With an ideal circular orbit and unchanged Earth-Moon masses, Kepler's third law predicts an orbital period around 9.7 days versus 27.32 today. This hypothetical is not a real forecast.

Sources:
NASA Moon facts, mean distance 384,400 km: https://science.nasa.gov/moon/facts/
NASA Moon fact sheet, sidereal period 27.3217 days: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/moonfact.html
NOAA on inverse-cube tide-generating forces: https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/education/tutorial_tides/tides02_cause.html
NASA on Kepler's third law: https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/orbits-and-keplers-laws/

Derived calculations: 384,400 / 2 = 192,200 km; (384,400 / 192,200)^3 = 8; 27.3217 × (0.5)^(3/2) ≈ 9.66 days.

Original graphics, synthetic narration. No real-world disaster or measured coastal tide height is asserted.

scenes.say: What if the Moon circled Earth at half its usual distance?
The Moon's tide-raising force would climb to roughly eight times today's.
Right now, its average distance is about three hundred eighty-four thousand kilometres.
At half the distance, roughly one hundred ninety-two thousand kilometres, the tide-generating pull changes dramatically.
Tidal forcing scales with the inverse cube of distance: half as far means eight times the force.
But this does not mean every beach sees water rise eight times higher.
